lesson.title: Reading the Far Edges of a Graph: End Behavior
lesson.summary: End behavior describes what a function does as x moves toward positive or negative infinity, and for polynomials it is controlled entirely by the single term with the highest power.
lesson.body:
End behavior is the general question of what happens to f(x) as x moves toward positive infinity and as x moves toward negative infinity, answered using the limit-at-infinity tools from the previous section, but now applied broadly rather than only to rational functions built for horizontal asymptotes. Some functions settle to a finite value, producing a horizontal asymptote, some grow or shrink without bound, and some oscillate forever. End behavior is the umbrella description covering all of these outcomes.

For polynomials specifically, end behavior is controlled entirely by the leading term, the term with the highest power of x, because as x grows large in magnitude, that single term dominates every other term in the sum. This is why the degree and the sign of the leading coefficient are often taught as a shortcut for sketching a polynomial's far left and far right behavior without any further computation.

For a worked example, take f(x) = -2x^3 + 5x^2 - 1. The leading term is -2x^3, an odd degree term with a negative coefficient. To see why it dominates, factor it out: f(x) = x^3 times (-2 + 5/x - 1/x^3). As x approaches infinity, 5/x approaches 0 and 1/x^3 approaches 0, so the bracketed factor approaches -2, and f(x) behaves like -2x^3 for large x. Since x^3 approaches positive infinity as x approaches infinity, and the coefficient is negative, f(x) approaches negative infinity as x approaches infinity. As x approaches negative infinity, x^3 approaches negative infinity, and multiplying by the negative coefficient flips the sign, so f(x) approaches positive infinity as x approaches negative infinity.

A numerical check confirms this. At x = 100, f(100) = -2(1,000,000) + 5(10,000) - 1 = -2,000,000 + 50,000 - 1 = -1,950,001, a large negative number, consistent with f(x) approaching negative infinity. At x = -100, f(-100) = -2(-1,000,000) + 5(10,000) - 1 = 2,000,000 + 50,000 - 1 = 2,049,999, a large positive number, consistent with f(x) approaching positive infinity. Notice how quickly the leading term takes over: even at a moderate input like 100, the -2x^3 contribution already swamps the 5x^2 term by more than an order of magnitude.

This leading-term-wins principle is really just an application of the limit-at-infinity technique: factor out the highest power and watch every other term vanish. It also explains a broader pattern: odd-degree polynomials with a positive leading coefficient go from negative infinity to positive infinity across their domain, guaranteeing at least one real root by the Intermediate Value Theorem, while even-degree polynomials have both ends pointing in the same direction. Non-polynomial functions follow their own end behavior rules, exponential functions eventually outgrow any polynomial, and rational functions combine numerator and denominator degrees as already seen, but the underlying question, and the underlying limit-at-infinity toolbox, is the same in every case.
